newsitem.title: USA: AT&T a latecomer on fixed rate pricing plan.
newsitem.headline: AT&T a latecomer on fixed rate pricing plan.

text.p: MCI Communications Corp said the company has signed up one million customers for its fixed-rate $0.15 a minute residential long distance calling plan in the one year since the service was introduced.
Separately, Sprint Corp, said its residential long distance business grew three times faster than AT&T's consumer business for each of the first two quarters of 1996.

The two AT&T Corp rivals were responding to AT&T's announcement Tuesday that it would offer its own fixed-rate, $0.15 per minute plan in a bid to simplify consumer pricing and stem market share losses in this core business segment.

"They are boldly going where MCI has gone before," said John Donahue, MCI's executive vice president for consumer services, of the AT&T program, the terms of which duplicate those of the MCIminutes program.
"We have over a million customers on (MCIminutes)," Donahue said in a phone interview.

Industry analysts said AT&T's conversion to flat rate pricing for residential customers was a defensive move to stem the giant carrier's market share losses to both Sprint and MCI, and additional nibbles by hundreds of smaller rivals.
Sprint spokesman Steve Lunceford said, "Sprint's consumer long distance business grew three times faster than AT&T's consumer business in the first and second quarter of 1996."
"Right now, in the third quarter, we are seeing Sprint Sense and the new promotion continuing to post gains."
Sprint pioneered fixed-rate calling among the major carriers with the dime-a-minute Sprint Sense program it introduced in January 1995.
The plan applies to evenings and weekends, periods when residential customers place 75 percent of their calls, according to a study of 1,000 consumers conducted by Sprint.
Daytime calls are billed at the rate of $0.22 per minute.
The promotion the spokesman mentioned is an additional plan that allows Sprint customers to place $0.10 a minute long distance calls day or night to a specific number, such as family member.
By contrast, MCI and now AT&T offer $0.15 per minute calling as a standard rate, 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
"We are very happy with what we have now," Lunceford said of its dime-a-minute, evenings and weekends plan and added that the company has no plans to change course.

Donahue said his company's MCIminutes plan offers the same terms for U.S. long distance calls made from home as those announced by AT&T earlier on Tuesday. The plan is in effect 24 hours a day and throughout the week.
The MCI executive said the fixed rate calling plan is just one of the options MCI offers consumers.
"The most important thing in this market is the targetting," Donahue said. "What we've found is that one size doesn't fit all."
MCI also offers its Friends and Family program, in which discounts apply to a circle of frequently called numbers.
He said his company has sought to sidestep the raw competition based on pricing alone by increasingly offering a bundle of related services to build customer loyalty and stem customer turnover.
"The key is integrated services," he said.

In a conference call with reporters earlier on Tuesday, Joseph Nacchio, AT&T executive vice president for consumer and small business services, outlined a similar plan to MCI's, coupling fixed-rate consumer pricing and new bundled services.
"We believe that consumers will be looking for more services, but with simplicity," he said.

Analysts said AT&T has been caught off guard in recent months by the market share losses to so-called "unknown competitors" small firms that provide customers with special codes to dial around AT&T or prepaid calling cards.
These firms have begun to wrest customers away from AT&T without actually requiring that customers quit using AT&T as their basic long distance provider, they said.
-- Eric Auchard, New York Newsdesk, 212-859-1736
